title: Finding out: planning a test and watching slow changes

summary.text: A cut apple slice turns brown, but nobody can see it happen. Look at it every ten minutes and draw it each time, and the change shows up clearly. To find something out, a scientist first makes a plan: the question, what to look at, what to compare, how often to look, and how to write it down. Some questions need one look. Others need many looks over minutes, days or years. In this unit you plan your own investigation, keep a record, and hear how Tycho Brahe's nightly measurements showed that even the sky can change.
summary.art: A white plate with three apple slices labelled plain, lemon and water, and beside it a child's notebook page with a row of small drawings of the slices, each with a time written under it.

intro.hook: Cut a slice of apple and put it on a plate. Now stare at it for one whole minute without looking away. Did it change? Leave it on the plate, and look again in half an hour.
intro.text: In half an hour the cut side has gone yellow or brown. Yet in the minute you stared, you saw nothing happen. The change was real, but too slow for one look. To catch a slow change, you need a plan: look again and again at set times, and write down what you see each time. That is how scientists watch things that change slowly, from a cut apple to a growing child to a star.
intro.art: A child sitting with chin on hands, staring hard at a pale apple slice on a plate, and the same slice beside a clock half an hour later, its cut face gone brown.

outcomes: I can turn something I wonder about into a question that looking or testing can answer.
I can plan how to find out: what to look at, what to compare, how often to look, how long, and how to write it down.
I can observe over time, writing the time, a drawing or score, and a few words at every look.
I can explain why a record kept over time catches slow changes that one look, or my memory, can miss.
I can explain why a cut apple turns brown, and why lemon juice and water slow it down.
I can tell how Tycho Brahe's measurements, night after night, showed that the sky can change.

terms.meaning: A question that looking, counting or testing can answer. 'Why is the sky?' is hard to answer by looking. 'Does a cut apple go brown faster in air or in water?' can be tested.
terms.example: 'Do more crows come to our window in the morning or in the afternoon?' You can find out by counting at both times for a week.
terms.art: Two speech bubbles from a child: one with a fuzzy cloud and a question mark, one with an apple slice, a clock and a tick.

terms.meaning: To look at something carefully, and use your other senses too: listen, touch, smell, and sometimes taste, if it is safe. An observation is one thing you noticed.
terms.example: Kavya observes an apple slice: 'The cut side is cream, wet and shiny. It smells sweet.'
terms.art: A child bending close to an apple slice with a magnifying glass, one hand cupped to an ear and the nose near the slice.

terms.meaning: What you write, draw or photograph at the time you observe, so you don't have to remember it later. A record always says when each observation was made.
terms.example: '4:10 pm. Plain slice: light yellow, score 1.' That line is a record.
terms.art: A notebook page with a neat table: a time column, a colour score column and small sketches of an apple slice.

terms.meaning: A guess about what will happen, made before you test, with a reason. 'I think the lemon slice will stay pale, because Amma puts lemon on cut apples' is a prediction with a reason.
terms.example: Before cutting the apple, Arjun predicts that the slice under water will stay pale longest.
terms.art: A child writing a guess on a slip of paper and folding it, before an apple is cut.

terms.meaning: The steps you decide on before you start finding out: your question, your guess and why, what you will look at, what you will compare, how often and how long you will look, and how you will write it down.
terms.example: Lakshmi's plan: 'Three slices. Look every 10 minutes for an hour. Give each a colour score from 0 to 3.'
terms.art: A plan written as five short lines on a card, with small pictures of a question mark, an apple, a clock, a pencil and a table.

terms.meaning: To look at two or more things side by side to see how they are the same and how they differ.
terms.example: We compare a plain apple slice with a slice that has lemon juice on it.
terms.art: Two apple slices side by side on a plate, one brown and one pale, with a child's finger pointing between them.

terms.meaning: A test where only one thing is different between the things you compare, and everything else is kept the same. Then any difference you see must come from that one thing.
terms.example: All three slices come from the same apple, are cut at the same time, and sit in the same room. Only plain, lemon or water is different.
terms.art: Three identical apple slices in a row with arrows showing the same knife, the same apple and the same room, and one different label each.

terms.meaning: Looking at the same thing again and again, at set times, and recording each look. It shows changes that are too slow to see in one look.
terms.example: Photographing the same banana every morning for five days shows it going from yellow to spotted to brown.
terms.art: Five pictures of one banana in a row, labelled Day 1 to Day 5, going from yellow to spotted brown.

terms.meaning: The time you wait between one look and the next. A fast change needs a short interval, and a slow change can have a long one.
terms.example: For an apple slice, an interval of 10 minutes works. For a banana, one day is enough.
terms.art: A clock face with two hands and a curved arrow marking a 10-minute gap between them.

terms.meaning: What you actually saw, counted or measured, which shows whether an idea is right. Evidence comes from the record, not from what you hoped would happen.
terms.example: 'The plain slice reached score 2 after 30 minutes, and the lemon slice stayed at 0.' That is evidence.
terms.art: A notebook page held up next to the three real apple slices, with the numbers matching the colours.

terms.meaning: A tiny helper made by living cells that speeds up one particular change. An apple's cells make an enzyme that helps turn colourless substances brown when they meet oxygen.
terms.example: The enzyme in a cut apple works fast at room temperature and slowly in the fridge.
terms.art: A zoomed-in drawing of a broken apple cell, with tiny round enzymes joining a colourless dot and an oxygen dot into a brown dot.

terms.meaning: A gas in the air all around us. We breathe it in. In a cut apple, oxygen from the air takes part in making the brown colour.
terms.example: A slice kept under water gets much less oxygen than a slice in the open air, and it browns more slowly.
terms.art: An apple slice on a plate with tiny dots of air drifting onto its cut face, and a second slice under water with only a few dots.

terms.meaning: A star that explodes. For weeks it can shine brighter than a whole galaxy of stars, and then it fades over months.
terms.example: The new star Tycho Brahe watched in 1572 was a supernova.
terms.art: A dark sky with a W-shaped group of stars and one very bright new star shining beside them.

explanations.context: This card is about the first step of finding out: asking a question that looking or testing can answer.
explanations.definition: A question you can find out is one that looking, counting, measuring or testing can answer. It names what you will look at, and what might change.
explanations.description: Children wonder about everything, and every wondering is worth keeping. Some wonderings are big and hard, like 'Why do apples exist?' Others can be turned into questions you can answer at home. 'Why does my apple go brown?' becomes 'Does a slice go brown faster in the open air, or under water?' The second question tells you what to do: cut two slices, put one in water, and watch both. A good question to find out is small, clear and about something you can see, count or measure. Big questions still matter. Scientists often answer a big question one small question at a time.
examples: 'Are ants clever?' is big. 'Do the ants on our kitchen wall find a grain of sugar faster than a grain of salt?' can be tested.
'Why does the banana go bad?' becomes 'Does a banana get more brown spots each day?' You can count the spots every morning.
'Do crows like our balcony?' becomes 'How many times does a crow land on our railing between 7 and 8 in the morning?'
explanations.art: A child's notebook with a big cloud of wonderings at the top, and arrows down to three small, clear questions, each with a tiny picture of what to look at.

explanations.concept: Making a plan before you start
explanations.context: This card says what goes into a plan for finding something out, and why each part matters.
explanations.definition: A plan answers these questions before you begin: What is my question? What do I guess, and why? What will I look at? What will I compare, and what will I keep the same? How often will I look, and for how long? How will I write it down? What do I need, and what must be done safely?
explanations.description: A plan saves you from finding out too late that you forgot something. If you don't write the start time, you can't say how long the change took. If you don't keep everything else the same, you can't say what caused a difference. If you only look at the start and the end, you miss when the change happened. Writing your guess first matters too. Once you have seen the result, it is easy to think 'I knew that all along.' A written guess keeps you honest, and a wrong guess is often the most interesting part.
examples: Divya forgot to label her slices, and after an hour she could not tell which one had lemon on it. Now she writes labels before she cuts.
A plan for a banana: 'Question: how fast do brown spots appear? Look each morning at 8. Same spot on the table, same light. Count spots and take a photo.'
Before the apple test, Farhan writes, 'I think the water slice will brown fastest, because water makes things go soggy.' He turns out to be wrong, and that is useful.
explanations.art: A card titled My Plan with seven short lines and small icons: a question mark, a thought bubble, an eye, a balance, a clock, a pencil and a pair of safety gloves.

explanations.context: This card is about watching one thing many times, so that slow changes show up.
explanations.definition: Observing over time means looking at the same thing again and again, at chosen times, in the same way each time, and recording each look.
explanations.description: Many changes are too slow for our eyes. An apple slice browns, a banana ripens, a child grows, and the Moon changes shape. If you stare, you see nothing happen. If you look at set times and record each look, the records lay the change out in a row, like frames of a film. Each look should be done the same way: from the same place, in the same light, judged on the same scale. Otherwise a change in the light might look like a change in the apple. A phone photo from the same spot each time is a very good record.
examples: A height mark on the door frame every birthday shows how much a child grew, though nobody saw them grow.

Maria Mitchell, an American astronomer, looked at the sky from her roof on clear nights. On 1 October 1847 she found a comet nobody had reported before. She knew it was new because she knew the sky so well.
India's weather scientists have written down the day the monsoon reaches Kerala every year for more than a hundred years. That long record shows how much the date changes from year to year.
explanations.art: A strip of six photos of the same apple slice, taken from the same spot, getting browner, with times from 0 to 50 minutes underneath.

explanations.context: This card is about choosing the gap between looks, called the interval.
explanations.definition: The interval is the time between one look and the next. Choose it to match how fast the thing changes, so that each look shows a small, clear step.
explanations.description: If the interval is too long, you miss the change. Look at an apple slice only once after a day, and you know it went brown, but not how fast. If the interval is too short, you waste effort and see no difference between looks. Checking a banana every ten minutes would show nothing new for hours. A useful rule: guess how long the whole change takes, and plan to look about 5 to 10 times in that time. An apple slice changes over about an hour, so look every 10 minutes. A banana changes over about a week, so look once a day.
examples: Apple slice: every 10 minutes for an hour.
Banana: every morning for five or six days.
The Moon's shape: every evening for a month.
explanations.art: A row of three clocks with different gaps marked: a short gap beside an apple slice, a one-day gap beside a banana, a one-week gap beside a growing plant.

explanations.concept: Why we write it down at the time
explanations.context: This card is about why scientists trust a record more than their memory.
explanations.definition: A record made at the time of looking is evidence. A memory, recalled later, can change without our noticing.
explanations.description: People often remember things wrongly, even things they saw clearly. Our memory fills gaps with what we expect, and our first guess can colour what we think we saw. Two people who watched the same thing often remember it differently. A record written at the moment you look does not change afterwards. It also lets someone else check your work, because they can read exactly what you saw and when. That is why every scientist keeps a notebook, and why Tycho Brahe wrote down every measurement he made.
examples: After an hour, ask someone what colour the plain slice was at the start. Then show them the first drawing. Many people remember it as darker than it was.
Two cricket fans watching the same catch often argue about whether it touched the ground. The replay settles it, because it is a record.
A doctor writes your temperature on a chart each time, rather than trusting how hot your forehead felt yesterday.
explanations.art: Two children arguing with different-coloured thought bubbles about an apple slice, and a notebook between them showing the real colour.

explanations.concept: Why a cut apple turns brown
explanations.context: This card explains what was happening to the apple slices in the main test.
explanations.definition: When an apple is cut, its cells break open. An enzyme from the cells helps colourless substances in the apple join with oxygen from the air. This makes new substances that are brown.
explanations.description: An apple is made of millions of tiny cells. Inside them are colourless substances, and in other parts of the cells there is an enzyme, a helper that speeds up one change. In a whole apple, these are kept apart, so the flesh stays cream. A knife breaks the cells, the two mix, and the oxygen in the air joins in. The brown appears first where the air touches the cut face. Under water, much less oxygen reaches the slice, so it browns slowly. Lemon juice is sour, or acidic, and this enzyme works slowly in acid. Lemon juice also has vitamin C, which undoes the first step of the browning. Cold slows the enzyme too, so a slice in the fridge browns more slowly. A brown apple slice is not rotten. It is safe to eat, though it may taste a little different.
examples: A cut potato, a cut brinjal and a peeled banana brown for the same reason.
Many cooks drop cut brinjal or potato into a bowl of water until they are ready to cook it.
A bitten apple browns around the tooth marks first, where the cells were broken.
explanations.art: A zoomed-in view of an apple's cut face: whole cells inside, and broken cells at the surface where colourless dots, enzyme dots and oxygen from the air meet and form brown.

explanations.concept: Why does an apple make brown at a cut?
explanations.context: This card asks how browning might help the apple tree, and what scientists still don't know.
explanations.description: An apple tree's fruit faces real problems. Insects bite into it, birds peck it, and germs, such as fungi and bacteria, try to get in through any wound. Many scientists think the browning is part of the fruit's defence. The brown substances, and the ones made just before them, can harm germs and insects and seal the wound a little, rather like a scab. In one experiment, tomato plants made to have less of this enzyme were harmed more by disease. But this is still being studied, and the enzyme may have other jobs in the plant too.
examples: Scientists have made a kind of apple that hardly browns, by switching off the gene for this enzyme.
Tea leaves and coffee beans turn brown by a similar change, and people use it on purpose to give them their flavour and colour.

perspectives.explanation: The browning helps defend a damaged fruit or leaf against insects and germs.
Defence is one job, but the enzyme probably has other jobs inside the healthy plant that we don't fully understand yet.

explanations.art: An apple hanging from a tree branch, with a small bite taken out of the fruit, the bite edge gone brown, and a fly and a speck of mould shown backing away.

explanations.concept: Tycho Brahe's plan: is the new star near or far?
explanations.context: This card explains the clever plan behind Tycho Brahe's measurements in 1572.
explanations.definition: A near thing seems to shift against far things when you look at it from a different place. A very far thing does not seem to shift. Scientists call this shift parallax.
explanations.description: Hold a pencil at arm's length and look past it at a far wall. Close one eye, then the other. The pencil seems to jump, but the wall does not. The Moon is fairly near us, so as the Earth turns through the night, the Moon seems to shift a little against the far stars. In 1572 Tycho Brahe saw a bright new star. Many people said it must be something in the air, nearer than the Moon. Tycho planned a test: if the new light was near, it would shift against its neighbour stars during the night. He measured its position again and again with a large instrument he had made. It never shifted. So it was far beyond the Moon, out among the stars. The sky, which people had said could never change, had changed.
examples: Your thumb jumps against the window frame when you swap eyes, but the far building does not.
From a moving train, nearby trees rush past, but a far hill seems to move slowly.
explanations.art: A night sky with a W-shaped group of stars and a bright new star beside it, a man measuring with a large wooden instrument, and an inset of a pencil jumping against a wall.

agreed.text: Scientists record observations at the time they make them, with the date and time, because memory can change.
agreed.evidence: Many studies have shown that people misremember events they saw, often with great confidence. Written records and photos do not change afterwards.

agreed.text: Looking again and again at set times shows changes that are too slow to see in one look.
agreed.evidence: Time-lapse photos show flowers opening, plants turning and clouds forming. Long records of rainfall, temperature and plant flowering show changes over many years.

agreed.text: A cut apple browns because an enzyme from its broken cells helps its colourless substances join with oxygen from the air.
agreed.evidence: Slices kept away from air, kept cold, or coated in acid such as lemon juice brown much more slowly. Scientists have found the enzyme and studied it in the lab.

agreed.text: The new star of 1572 was a supernova, an exploding star far beyond the Moon.
agreed.evidence: Tycho Brahe found no shift against the other stars. Today, telescopes can see the cloud of gas left by that explosion, in the same place in the sky.

challenging.claim: Scientists just look carefully, and the answer comes to them.
challenging.who: A common idea about how science works
challenging.for: Some discoveries did start with someone noticing something by chance.
challenging.against: Noticing is only the start. To find out what is really going on, scientists plan what to look at, what to compare and when to look, and they write it all down. Even Tycho Brahe's first sight of the new star needed a planned test to show how far away it was.
challenging.context: This card is about a common picture of science as just looking.

challenging.claim: If I watch carefully, I will remember what I saw. I don't need to write it down.
challenging.for: We do remember a lot of what we see, especially if it surprised us.
challenging.against: Memory fills gaps with what we expect, and changes as time passes. Two careful watchers often remember the same thing differently. A record made at the time settles it.
challenging.context: This card is about trusting memory instead of a record.

challenging.claim: A brown apple slice has gone bad and should be thrown away.
challenging.for: Food that goes brown and soft is often rotten, so brown can look like a warning.
challenging.against: Browning is a change in the apple's own substances, made with oxygen from the air. It happens within minutes, long before germs could spoil the fruit. A brown slice is safe to eat. Mould, a bad smell or slime are signs of rotting.
challenging.context: This card is about whether browning means rotting.

challenging.claim: Lemon juice keeps an apple pale because it covers the slice and keeps the air out.
challenging.for: Lemon juice does coat the slice.
challenging.against: Water coats a slice too, but in the air a wet slice still browns. Lemon works mainly because it is sour, or acidic, and the browning enzyme works slowly in acid. Its vitamin C also undoes the first step of browning.
challenging.context: This card is about why lemon juice works.

challenging.claim: The sky beyond the Moon is perfect and never changes.
challenging.who: Aristotle, a Greek thinker, about 350 BCE, and many people in Europe for about 2,000 years after him
challenging.for: The stars do keep the same patterns year after year, so the sky looks unchanging.
challenging.against: In 1572 Tycho Brahe measured a new star and showed it was far beyond the Moon. Astronomers in China had recorded such 'guest stars' for more than a thousand years, and they recorded this one too. Today we know stars are born, change and die.
challenging.context: This card is about an old idea that Tycho Brahe's measurements helped overturn.

big_questions.q: Your apple slice looked still, but it was changing. Is anything in your room really still, or is everything changing too slowly to see?
big_questions.hint: Think about a wall, a steel tumbler, a plant and yourself. What would you see if you photographed each one every day for a hundred years?

big_questions.q: If nobody looks at the apple slice, does it still turn brown?
big_questions.hint: Leave a slice in a closed room and look only after an hour. What does that tell you?

big_questions.q: Why did nobody see the apple change, even though it changed while they watched?
big_questions.hint: How big was the change in one minute? Could your eyes notice a change that small?

big_questions.q: You are growing all the time, but you don't notice yourself growing. Are you the same person you were as a baby?
big_questions.hint: Look at a baby photo of yourself. What has changed? What has stayed the same?

big_questions.q: Tycho Brahe trusted his measurements more than the words of a famous thinker. When should we trust what we see over what we are told?
big_questions.hint: What made Tycho's measurements strong? Could he have been wrong too?

big_questions.q: Some changes take longer than a whole human life, like a mountain wearing down. How could people ever find out about them?
big_questions.hint: Think about records that are passed on, like a notebook kept by a grandmother and then her granddaughter.

story.title: The Pencil Line on the Wall
story.note: The story is made up. What Dadi does is true: engineers check whether a crack is growing by marking its ends with a pencil line and the date, and by fixing a thin strip, called a tell-tale, across it. If the crack moves, the strip tears or shifts. Low light from the side makes cracks look deeper and darker.
text: It had rained all afternoon in Hyderabad. Farzana was nine, and she was sitting on the balcony floor, drawing the rain. Her little brother Imran was lining up his toy autos along the railing.
Abba came out with his tea and stopped. He bent close to the wall beside the balcony door. A thin, dark crack ran down from the corner of the door frame, as long as a pencil.
"Look at this," Abba said. "This crack is getting bigger. It was tiny last year. The building is moving."
Ammi came to the door, drying her hands. "That crack has been there since we moved in," she said. "It was always that long."
"It was not," said Abba. "I remember it. It was half this size."
"I remember it too," said Ammi. "It was just the same."
Farzana looked from one to the other. They both sounded very sure. But they could not both be right.

Dadi was sitting in her chair by the window, reading the newspaper. For forty years she had worked as an engineer for the city, checking bridges and old buildings. She folded the paper and came over slowly.
"You both remember it differently," she said. "So which memory should we trust?"
Nobody answered.
"Neither," said Dadi. "Memory is a poor ruler. It stretches and shrinks without telling you. Let's ask the wall instead."
"How can you ask a wall?" said Imran.
Dadi smiled. "You make a plan, and you write down what it tells you. Farzana, bring your pencil and your drawing book."
Farzana fetched them. Dadi sat on the low stool by the crack.
"First, what exactly is our question?" Dadi asked.
Farzana thought. "Is the crack getting bigger?"
"Bigger how? Longer, or wider, or both?"
"Both," said Farzana. "So we have to watch the ends, to see if it gets longer. And the widest part, to see if it gets wider."
"Good. Draw a short pencil line across the crack, just past each end. Write today's date next to each line."
Farzana drew two small lines, one at the top and one at the bottom, and wrote the date in tiny numbers.
"If the crack grows past a line, we will know it got longer," said Farzana.

"Now the width." Dadi tore a thin strip of paper, about as long as a finger. She glued it across the widest part of the crack, one end on each side. "Engineers call this a tell-tale, because it tells tales. If the crack opens wider, it pulls the two sides apart, and the paper tears."
"How often do we look?" Farzana asked.
"Cracks change slowly, if they change at all. Looking every hour would show nothing. Once a week is enough. And after every heavy rain, because water can make walls swell and move."

Farzana made a table in her drawing book. Date. Top end past the line? Bottom end past the line? Paper strip torn? Notes. Then she took a photo of the crack with Ammi's phone, with a one-rupee coin stuck beside it with tape, so she could tell its size later.
"Always from the same spot," said Dadi. "And in the morning light, each time."

Every Sunday morning, Farzana checked the crack. The first Sunday, nothing had changed. The second Sunday, nothing had changed. The third Sunday, Imran said, "This is the most boring science in the world."
"Nothing changing is an answer too," said Dadi. "Write it down."

In the fourth week, a storm blew in from the east and the rain lashed the balcony for a whole night. The next morning Farzana ran out before breakfast. The paper strip had gone wrinkly from the damp. But it was not torn. The top end of the crack was still above the pencil line. The bottom end was still above the other one. She wrote it all down.
After six weeks, Farzana carried her drawing book to the dining table, where Abba was reading.
"Abba, look. Six Sundays and one storm. The crack did not get longer. It did not get wider. The paper never tore." She showed him the photos side by side. They looked exactly the same.
Abba studied the page for a long time. "Then why did it look so much bigger to me that evening?"
"What time was it?" asked Dadi.
"Evening. The sun was low, after the rain."
"Low light from the side fills every crack with shadow," said Dadi. "Cracks always look deeper and darker in evening light. That's one reason I check in the same light each time."
Abba laughed. "So my memory was wrong, and my eyes fooled me too. Your book is better than both of them."
"What if it does start to grow one day?" asked Farzana.
"Then your book will tell us early," said Dadi, "and we will call an engineer who still climbs ladders."

So Farzana kept checking, once a month now. Imran gave up on the crack. But he did draw a pencil line on the door frame at the top of his head, with the date beside it. "That's my tell-tale," he said. "Next year it will show how much I grew."
story.epiphany: For the parent: Abba and Ammi both trusted their memories, and their memories disagreed. Neither could be checked, so neither could settle the question. Farzana's plan turned the argument into something you could look at: pencil lines at the ends to show any lengthening, a paper strip across the crack to show any widening, the same time and light each week, and a record. The record showed no change, and 'no change' is a real result. It also explained why Abba was fooled: low evening light makes cracks look larger. Imran's height mark at the end is the same idea used for something that really does change.
ask: Abba and Ammi remembered the crack differently. Why couldn't they settle who was right?
Why did Farzana draw lines past both ends of the crack, and not just one?
What was the paper strip for? What would it have shown if the crack got wider?
Why did Dadi say once a week was enough, and not every hour?
Imran said nothing changing was boring. Dadi said it was an answer too. Who do you agree with, and why?
Why did Dadi always check in the morning light?

games.title: Spot the Change: memory or record?
games.context: This is a looking game about a tray of small things. One player changes the tray while the other looks away. Players find out whether a quick look and a memory, or a drawing made at the time, catches more changes.

printables.title: A tray grid: a sheet with 9 squares to lay things on
items: A sheet of paper with 9 squares drawn in 3 rows of 3, each square about the size of a palm

printables.title: 12 change cards to cut out, for the changer
items: Swap two things
Turn one thing upside down
Take one thing away
Add one new thing
Move one thing to an empty square
Turn the spoon to point the other way
Open or close the box
Put the coin on its other side
Roll the rubber band into a ball
Swap a thing for one that looks almost the same
Move one thing a little, inside its square
Change nothing at all (a trick card)

printables.title: Score sheet
items: Round
Memory round: changes found
Drawing round: changes found
Changes really made

rules: Lay 7 small things from home on the tray grid: for example a steel spoon, a one-rupee coin, a pencil, a bindi packet, a rubber band, a matchbox and a button.
Memory round: the looker studies the tray for 30 seconds, then turns away. The changer picks 2 change cards and makes those changes. The looker turns back and says what changed.

Drawing round: the looker studies the tray for 30 seconds and draws a quick map of it on the 9 squares, with arrows for which way things point. Then the changer makes 2 new changes. The looker checks the tray against the drawing.
Score 1 point for each change found. Write the scores on the score sheet.
Play 3 memory rounds and 3 drawing rounds, then compare the totals.
Playing alone with a parent: the parent is always the changer.

flow.do: 1. Lay the 9-square sheet on a table. 2. Put 7 small things on it, one in each of 7 squares. 3. Shuffle the change cards face down.
flow.say: This game tests two ways of remembering. First you'll use only your memory. Then you'll make a quick drawing. Which do you think will catch more changes?
flow.kid: Put seven small things on the squares. Mix up the cards. Which will win, your memory or a drawing? Guess first.

ask.q: Which do you think will catch more changes, your memory or a drawing? Why?
good: The drawing, because I can check it.
My memory, because I'm good at remembering.

flow.context: This is the first step of Spot the Change. You set up a tray of small things and guess which way of remembering works better.

flow.do: 1. Play 3 memory rounds. 2. In each, the looker studies the tray for 30 seconds and turns away. 3. The changer makes the changes on 2 cards. 4. The looker says what changed. Write the score.
flow.say: Look for 30 seconds. Now turn around. No peeking. Right, turn back. What changed?
flow.kid: Look at the tray for 30 seconds. Turn around. Now look again. What changed? Say it out loud.
flow.parent: Use some easy changes and some small ones, like turning the coin over or moving a thing a little inside its square. Small changes are where memory fails. Use the trick card once. It is a fair test of whether the looker invents a change that never happened.

flow.do: 1. Play 3 drawing rounds. 2. The looker studies the tray for 30 seconds and draws a quick map on paper, with arrows for which way things point. 3. The changer makes 2 changes. 4. The looker checks the tray against the drawing. Write the score.
flow.say: This time you can draw a quick map of the tray before you turn away. Show which way the spoon points and which side of the coin is up.
flow.kid: Now draw a quick map of the tray. Show which way things point. Turn around. Then check the tray against your drawing.

check.q: In the drawing rounds, most players catch more changes. Why?
options: The drawing was made at the time and does not change, so you can check against it
check.why: A drawing made while you look is a record. It stays the same, so you can compare the tray with it, point by point. Memory blurs small details and sometimes invents changes that never happened. Your eyes are no sharper in the drawing round, and the changes were just as hard.

flow.do: Add up the scores for the memory rounds and the drawing rounds. Compare them.
flow.say: Let's add up. Which way found more changes? Was your first guess right?
flow.kid: Add up your points for each kind of round. Which won? Was your guess right?
flow.think: Scientists write things down at the time they see them. After this game, can you say why?

games.title: One Look or Long Watch? A question sorting game
games.context: This is a card game about questions. Players sort question cards by how you would find out the answer: with one look, by watching over time, by doing a test, or by asking someone or reading.

printables.title: 20 question cards to cut out
items: What colour is the inside of a cucumber? (One look)
How many legs does an ant have? (One look, with a hand lens)
Does our banana get more brown spots each day? (Long watch)
Does the Moon look the same shape every night? (Long watch)
How much does a moong sprout grow in a week? (Long watch)
When does the sunny patch reach the far wall of the room? (Long watch)
Does a cut apple brown faster in the fridge or on the table? (Test)
Does sugar dissolve faster in hot water or cold water? (Test)
Which of our chappals grips best on a wet floor? (Test)
Does a paper boat float longer if it is folded twice? (Test)
What did Paati eat for breakfast when she was a girl? (Ask)
How far away is the Sun? (Read)
How many crows land on our railing between 7 and 8 in the morning? (Long watch)
Is the steel tumbler colder than the wooden table? (One look and touch)
Does a curry leaf plant grow towards the window? (Long watch)
Does our tap drip faster at night? (Long watch)
Which dries faster on the clothesline, a thick towel or a thin cotton dupatta? (Test)
How many seeds are inside one tomato? (One look, and counting)
What will the weather be like on my birthday next year? (Hard to find out by looking)
What does a crow dream about? (Hard to find out by looking)

printables.title: A sorting mat with 5 boxes
items: One look
Long watch
Test
Ask or read
Hard to find out by looking

rules: Shuffle the question cards and put them face down. Cover the answers in brackets with a strip of paper, or fold them under.
On your turn, pick up a card and read the question out loud.
Put it in a box on the sorting mat, and say why. For a long watch, say how often you would look. For a test, say what you would compare.
The other players can agree or argue. Then check the answer in brackets.
Score 1 point for the right box, and 1 more for a good reason.
Some questions fit two boxes. If you can argue well for your box, you keep the point.

flow.do: 1. Lay out the sorting mat. 2. Shuffle the 20 cards with the answers hidden.
flow.say: Every question has its own way of being answered. Some need one look. Some need a test. Some need watching over days. Let's sort them.
flow.kid: Lay out the mat with five boxes. Mix up the cards. You will sort questions by how to find the answer.
flow.context: This is the first step of One Look or Long Watch. It is a card game where you sort questions by the way you would find the answer.

flow.do: Play the card 'Does our banana get more brown spots each day?' as a practice round.
flow.say: Practice card. Does our banana get more brown spots each day? Which box?
flow.kid: Practice card. Does our banana get more brown spots each day? Which box? Tap your answer.

check.q: Does our banana get more brown spots each day? Which box does this go in?
check.why: One look today would only show today's spots. To see if the spots increase each day, you must look every day, at the same time, and count. Asking someone gives you their memory, not a count.

flow.do: Take turns with the rest of the cards. For each long watch, the player says how often they would look. For each test, they say what they would compare.
flow.say: Long watch? How often would you look, and for how long? Test? What would you compare?
flow.kid: Pick a card. Read it. Put it in a box. Say why. Long watch? Say how often you would look.
flow.parent: The best talk comes from cards that fit two boxes. 'When does the sunny patch reach the far wall?' could be a long watch on one day, or you could ask someone who has noticed. Let your child argue. A good reason is worth more than the right box.

flow.do: Look at the two cards in 'Hard to find out by looking'. Talk about them.
flow.say: These two are in the hard box. Could anyone ever find out the answers? How might they try?
flow.kid: Look at the hard box. Could anyone ever find out these? How might they try?
flow.think: Weather scientists do try to say what the weather will be. How far ahead do you think they can?

experiments.title: The Brown Apple Watch
experiments.context: In this experiment you plan a test, cut three apple slices, and watch them for an hour. One is left plain, one has lemon juice on it, and one is kept under water. Every 10 minutes you score and draw each slice.
experiments.question: Does a cut apple slice turn brown fastest in the open air, with lemon juice on it, or under water?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Which slice will turn brown fastest, and which will stay pale longest? Why do you think so? Write your guess and your reason before you cut the apple.
experiments.fair_test: Cut all three slices from the same apple, at the same time, about as thick as a pencil. Keep them in the same room, out of direct sun. Only one thing is different: plain, lemon or water. Score every slice at the same times, using the same colour scale and the same light.

materials.item: one apple, any kind (red Shimla or Kashmiri apples brown well)
half a lemon
a steel bowl with a cup of water in it, and a small steel plate or katori that fits inside to keep a slice under water
a white plate
a knife and a chopping board, for a grown-up
three small paper labels: plain, lemon, water
a colour scale card you make: four boxes coloured with crayons or sketch pens, labelled 0 cream, 1 pale yellow, 2 light brown, 3 brown
a clock, or a phone timer
a notebook and pencil
a phone camera, if you have one (not needed)

experiments.safety: A grown-up cuts the apple. The slices are safe to eat afterwards, even the brown one.

schedule.what: Write a plan and a guess. Cut three slices. Score and draw them at 0, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 and 60 minutes. Compare the drawings.

experiments.record: Fill in the table at every look. Draw each slice small, in a row, with the time under each drawing.

flow.do: 1. Make the colour scale card with your child. 2. Draw the results table in the notebook. 3. Ask for a guess and a reason, and write both down.
flow.say: Before we cut anything, let's plan. Our question is which slice browns fastest. We'll look every 10 minutes for an hour. Which slice do you think will brown fastest? Why?
flow.kid: Make your colour card: 0, 1, 2, 3. Draw your table. Which slice will go brown first? Why? Write it down.

ask.q: Which slice do you think will brown fastest, and why?
good: The plain one, because the air touches it.
The water one, because water makes things soggy.
The lemon one, because lemon is strong.

flow.parent: Any guess is fine, as long as it has a reason. Don't hint. A wrong guess written down is a very good start, because the test will surprise your child.
flow.context: This is the first step of the brown apple watch. Here you make a plan and write your guess before anything is cut.

flow.do: 1. Cut three slices from the same apple, each about as thick as a pencil. 2. Put one on the plate by the label 'plain'. 3. Rub lemon juice over both sides of the second, and put it by the label 'lemon'. 4. Put the third in the bowl of water, with the small plate on top to keep it under. 5. Write the time.
flow.say: Now I'll cut three slices quickly, so they all start at the same time. Lemon juice goes on this one. This one goes under water. Let's write the start time.
flow.kid: A grown-up cuts three slices. Put one by 'plain'. Rub lemon on one. Put one under water. Write the time now.
flow.parent: Apple slices float, so the small plate or katori on top matters. Without it, the top of the slice sticks out into the air and browns. Cut fast, so all three start within a minute of each other.

flow.do: 1. Look at all three slices. 2. Hold each next to the colour card and give it a score. 3. Draw each one small in the notebook, with '0 minutes' under it. 4. Smell and touch the plain slice.
flow.say: This is our first look, at 0 minutes. Hold each slice next to the colour card. What score is it? How does it smell? How does it feel?
flow.kid: Look at each slice next to your colour card. What score? Draw it. Smell it. Touch it. Write 0 minutes.
flow.parent: Take the water slice out for a few seconds to score it, then put it straight back under the plate. All three should score 0 now.

flow.do: Ask your child to stare at the plain slice for one full minute, without looking away.
flow.say: Let's try something. Stare at the plain slice for one whole minute. Tell me the moment you see it change.
flow.kid: Stare at the plain slice for one whole minute. Shout when you see it change!

check.q: You stared at the plain slice for one minute. What did you see?
options: It went brown while I watched
It looked the same the whole minute
It went brown, then pale again
check.why: Most people see no change at all in one minute, even though the slice is changing. The change in one minute is too small for our eyes. That is why we look every 10 minutes and compare the drawings. If you thought you saw it go brown, check your next drawing: one minute rarely makes a visible difference.

flow.do: 1. Every 10 minutes, for an hour, score and draw all three slices. 2. Write the time and the scores in the table each time. 3. Between looks, do something else, like reading the Tycho Brahe card.
flow.say: It's 10 minutes. Time to look again. Same light, same colour card. What scores now?
flow.kid: Every 10 minutes, look again. Score each slice. Draw it. Write the time. Then go and do something else.
flow.parent: Each look takes about 2 minutes, so six looks take about 12 minutes, spread over an hour. Look in the same place and light each time. Light from a window changes through the day, so a lamp you switch on for each look gives the fairest light. If after an hour the plain slice still looks pale, your apple is a slow-browning kind. Leave it two more hours and look again, or try the same test with a slice of raw potato, which browns faster.

flow.do: 1. Lay the drawings side by side. 2. Ask your child to say what they think happened, what they saw, and why. 3. Read the explanation card on why a cut apple browns.
flow.say: Let's lay the drawings in a row. Which slice browned fastest? What did your record show that staring didn't? Now, why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Look at your drawings in a row. Which slice went brown fastest? Was your guess right? Why do you think it happened?

ask.q: What did you think, what did you see, and why do you think it happened?
good: I thought the water one would brown first. But the plain one did. The air touched it most.
The lemon slice stayed at 0. Lemon must stop the browning.

check.q: The plain slice browned and the water slice stayed paler. What does this tell us?
options: Something in the air helps the apple turn brown
The plain slice was from a different apple
check.why: The only difference between those two slices was air or water around them. The slice in the air browned faster, so something in the air helps. That something is oxygen. The water slice got much less oxygen. They came from the same apple, so a different apple can't explain it.

flow.parent: Expect the plain slice to brown most and the lemon slice least. The water slice is usually in between, browning slowly. Lemon juice is sour, and the enzyme that makes the brown works slowly in sour juice. Water keeps out most of the oxygen.

flow.do: Let your child taste a small bite of each slice, if they want to.
flow.say: All three are safe to eat. Does the brown one taste different? Does the lemon one?
flow.kid: You can taste each slice. They are all safe. Does the brown one taste different?
flow.think: If nobody had looked at the apple for an hour, would it still have gone brown?

experiments.title: Plan Your Own Apple Test
experiments.context: In this experiment you plan a new apple test yourself. You choose one thing to change, write the whole plan, and then do it. Nobody tells you the answer first.
experiments.question: Pick one: does a slice brown more slowly in the fridge? In salty water? Under an upside-down steel bowl? Your plan answers the one you pick.
experiments.predict: Before you start, write what you think will happen to your two slices, and why you think so.
experiments.fair_test: Two slices from the same apple, cut at the same time, the same thickness. One is your 'normal' slice on a plate on the table. The other gets your one change. Everything else stays the same, and you score both at the same times with the same colour card.

materials.item: one apple
for the fridge test: a small plate that fits in the fridge
for the salt test: a steel bowl of water with a pinch of salt stirred in, and a small katori to keep the slice under
for the bowl test: a steel bowl to turn upside down over the slice
the colour scale card from the brown apple watch
a knife, for a grown-up
a notebook and pencil, and a clock

schedule.what: Write the plan. Cut two slices. Score both every 10 minutes for an hour. Compare.

experiments.record: Write your plan on one page and your results table on the next. Draw both slices at every look.

flow.do: Help your child choose one change and write a plan with these headings: My question. My guess and why. What I change. What I keep the same. How often I look, and for how long. How I record it.
flow.say: This time you're the scientist who makes the plan. Choose one change. Then write each part of your plan. I'll only check that nothing is missing.
flow.kid: Choose one change: fridge, salty water, or a bowl on top. Write your question. Write your guess and why. Write what stays the same.

ask.q: What will you keep the same for both slices?
good: The same apple.
Cut at the same time.
The same thickness.
The same colour card and the same light.

flow.parent: Let your child make the choices, even if you think a choice won't work well. If they forget to write how often they will look, ask 'When will you look?' rather than telling them. Every 10 minutes for an hour works. For the fridge test, take the slice out only for the few seconds it takes to score it, because warming it changes the test.
flow.context: This is the first step of planning your own apple test. You write the whole plan yourself before anything is cut.

flow.do: Cut two slices at the same time. Put the normal slice on the plate on the table and give the other slice its change. Write the start time.
flow.say: Two slices, cut at the same moment. Which one gets the change? Write the time.
flow.kid: A grown-up cuts two slices. Put one on the plate. Give the other your change. Write the time.

flow.do: Every 10 minutes for an hour, score and draw both slices, and write the time.
flow.say: Time for a look. Score both slices with the colour card. Draw them. Write the time.
flow.kid: Every 10 minutes, score both slices. Draw them. Write the time.
flow.parent: In the fridge test, the cold slice usually browns much more slowly. In salty water, the slice usually stays pale. Under an upside-down bowl, there is still air, so the slice usually browns almost as fast as the open one. Your child does not know this yet, so don't say it.

flow.do: Compare the two rows of drawings. Ask what your child found, and whether the plan worked.
flow.say: What did your test show? Did your plan work? Is there anything you would change if you did it again?
flow.kid: What did your test show? Was your guess right? What would you change next time?

check.q: Kavya tested a slice under an upside-down steel bowl. It browned almost as fast as her open slice. Why?
options: There was still air with oxygen inside the bowl
check.why: A bowl over a slice doesn't take the air away. The air trapped inside still has plenty of oxygen for the browning. A slice under water gets much less oxygen. If you thought the steel mattered, you could test it with a glass bowl too.

activities.title: From Wondering to a Question
activities.context: This is a quick starter. You write down things you wonder about, then turn some of them into questions you could find out at home.

materials.item: a notebook and pencil

schedule.what: Write five wonderings. Turn two into questions you can find out.

activities.record: Write the five wonderings, then the two new questions underneath.

flow.do: 1. Walk around the flat for two minutes with your child. 2. Each of you notices things and says 'I wonder…'. 3. Write down five wonderings.
flow.say: Let's walk around the house and say 'I wonder' about anything we notice. Any wondering is good. I'll go first. I wonder why the fruit bowl bananas get spots.
flow.kid: Walk around your home. Look at things. Say 'I wonder…' about anything. Write down five.
flow.parent: Wonderings can be anything: 'I wonder why the fan wobbles', 'I wonder where the ants go'. Don't judge them. Write them in your child's words.
flow.context: This is the first step of From Wondering to a Question. You collect five things you wonder about.

flow.do: Pick two wonderings together. For each, ask: what could we look at, count or test to find out something about this? Write the new question.
flow.say: Let's make two of these into questions we could find out. Think about the spots on our bananas. We could ask whether the bananas get more spots each day. What could we look at or count?
flow.kid: Pick two wonderings. What could you look at or count? Write a question you can find out.

check.q: Which question can you find out at home by looking or testing?
options: Do ants come to a grain of sugar faster than a grain of salt?
check.why: The sugar and salt question says what to do and what to watch: put down both grains and see which one ants reach first. The other two are real and interesting questions. But looking alone can't answer them, so scientists would break them into smaller questions first.

flow.do: Keep the page. Some of these questions can become the child's own investigation later.
flow.say: Let's keep these. One of them might be your next investigation.
flow.kid: Keep this page. One of these could be your next test.

activities.title: Draw It Twice: memory and looking
activities.context: In this activity you draw a leaf twice: once from memory, and once while looking closely. Then you compare the two drawings.

materials.item: a leaf from a potted plant or a curry leaf, tulsi or money plant leaf from the kitchen
paper and pencil
a magnifying glass, if you have one

activities.safety: Pick a leaf you know is safe to touch. Wash hands afterwards.

schedule.what: Draw a leaf from memory. Then draw it while looking. Compare.

activities.record: Put both drawings side by side and write three things the looking drawing has that the memory drawing doesn't.

flow.do: Without showing the leaf, ask your child to draw a curry leaf or tulsi leaf from memory.
flow.say: Draw a curry leaf from memory. You've seen hundreds of them. Put in everything you remember.
flow.kid: Draw a curry leaf from memory. Put in everything you remember.
flow.context: This is the first step of Draw It Twice. You draw a leaf from memory before looking at a real one.

flow.do: Give your child the real leaf, and the magnifying glass if you have one. Ask them to draw it again, looking closely. Remind them to use touch and smell too.
flow.say: Now here's a real one. Look closely. Draw it again. Look at the edge, the lines, the stalk. Touch it. Smell it.
flow.kid: Now look at a real leaf. Draw it again. Look at the edge. Look at the lines. Touch it. Smell it.
flow.parent: A curry leaf is really a small leaflet. On the stem there are many leaflets in two rows. Children usually notice the pattern of lines, called veins, only when they look. Crushing a corner gives the smell.

flow.do: Put the two drawings side by side. Ask what the second one has that the first one is missing.
flow.say: Compare your two drawings. What did your memory leave out?
flow.kid: Put your two drawings side by side. What did your memory leave out?

ask.q: What did you notice only when you looked?
good: The veins.
The wavy edge.
One side is a bit bigger.
The smell when I crushed it.

activities.title: Window Watch: one minute every two hours
activities.context: In this activity you look out of the same window for one minute, every two hours through one day, and tally what you see.

materials.item: a window or balcony
a tally sheet with rows for each time and columns for crows, pigeons, people, vehicles and a column for the light
a clock or phone timer

activities.safety: Stay inside the window or behind the balcony railing.

schedule.what: At about 7, 9, 11, 1, 3, 5 and 7 o'clock, look out of the same window for one minute and tally what you see.

activities.record: The tally sheet, with the time written at each row.

flow.do: 1. Choose one window. 2. Make the tally sheet together. 3. Set a reminder every two hours.
flow.say: We'll be scientists of our window today. Every two hours, we look for exactly one minute and make tally marks. What do you think will change through the day?
flow.kid: Pick one window. Make your tally sheet. Every two hours, look for one minute. What will change?

ask.q: What do you think will change through the day? Why?
good: More cars in the morning, because people go to work.
More crows in the morning.
The light changes.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Window Watch. You plan a day of short looks from one window.

flow.do: At each time, look out of the same window for one minute, and make tally marks. Write a word about the light.
flow.say: One minute starts now. Tally every crow, pigeon, person and vehicle you see.
flow.kid: Look for one minute. Make a mark for every crow, pigeon, person and car. Write about the light.
flow.parent: Keep it to exactly one minute each time, using a timer. That makes the counts fair to compare. If you miss a time, write 'missed' rather than guessing.

flow.do: In the evening, look at the whole sheet together. What changed through the day?
flow.say: Look at the whole day. When were there most people? Most crows? Could one day be a fluke?
flow.kid: Look at your whole day. When did you see the most? Would tomorrow be the same?
flow.think: To be sure about a pattern, how many days would you need to watch?

activities.title: The Pencil Jump: Tycho's near-or-far test
activities.context: In this quick activity you see for yourself the trick Tycho Brahe used: a near thing seems to jump against far things when you change where you look from.

materials.item: a pencil
a window or a wall with something on it far away, like a door or a building

schedule.what: Hold up a pencil, swap eyes, and see the near pencil jump while far things stay still.

activities.record: Draw where the pencil seemed to be with the left eye, and with the right eye.

flow.do: 1. Hold a pencil at arm's length in front of a window. 2. Close your left eye, then open it and close your right eye. 3. Do it again with the pencil close to your nose.
flow.say: Hold the pencil out. Close one eye. Now swap. Does the pencil seem to jump? Does the building outside jump?
flow.kid: Hold the pencil out far. Close one eye. Swap eyes. Does the pencil jump? Does the far building jump?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Pencil Jump. You see how near things seem to jump when you look from a different place.

flow.do: Talk about what it means for Tycho's new star.
flow.say: Your two eyes are in different places. A near thing seems to jump. A far thing doesn't. Tycho looked for a jump like this in his new star.
flow.kid: A near thing jumps. A far thing doesn't. Tycho looked for a jump in his new star.

check.q: Tycho measured the new star many times. It never seemed to move against the stars near it. What did that show?
options: The star was very near, in the air
The star was very far away, beyond the Moon
check.why: Like the far building, a very far thing does not seem to jump. The Moon is near enough to shift a little against the stars through the night. The new star did not shift at all, so it had to be much further away than the Moon. His instrument worked well: it showed the shift for nearer things.

activities.title: Same Spot, Same Time: a week of photos
activities.context: In this activity you take one photo of the same view from the same spot at the same time every day for a week. Then you look at them in a row to see what changed.

materials.item: a phone camera
a piece of tape to mark where you stand

activities.safety: Take the photo from inside a window or behind the balcony railing.

schedule.what: Choose a view, mark where you stand with tape, and take the first photo.
Take the photo from the tape mark at the same time.
Take the photo from the tape mark at the same time.
Take the photo from the tape mark at the same time.
Take the photo from the tape mark at the same time.
Take the photo from the tape mark at the same time.
Take the last photo, then look at all seven in a row and list the changes.

activities.record: Seven photos in order, and a list of every change you can find between the first and the last.

flow.do: 1. Choose a view: a tree outside the window, a potted plant, or the fruit bowl. 2. Put tape on the floor where your child stands. 3. Take the first photo and note the time.
flow.say: Every day this week, at this same time, you'll stand on this tape and take one photo. Why do you think we use the same spot and the same time?
flow.kid: Stand on the tape. Take a photo of your view. Do it every day at this time.

ask.q: Why the same spot and the same time?
good: So the only change is in the view.
So the light is the same.
So the photos match.

flow.context: This is the first step of Same Spot, Same Time. You pick a view and take the first of seven daily photos.

flow.do: Each day, take the photo from the tape mark at the same time.
flow.say: Photo time. Stand on the tape.
flow.kid: Stand on the tape. Take today's photo.
flow.wait: Take one photo each day for the next five days.

flow.do: On day 7, take the last photo. Look at all seven in a row with your child. List every change.
flow.say: Let's look at all seven. What changed? What changed so slowly you never noticed it day to day?
flow.kid: Look at all seven photos in a row. What changed? List everything.
flow.parent: A fruit bowl changes a lot in a week. A tree may show new leaves, flowers, fruit or a nest. Clouds, washing on lines and parked cars also change, and that's worth noticing: some things change slowly and some change fast.

projects.title: One Banana, Five Days
projects.context: In this 5-day project you plan and keep a diary of one banana as it ripens. Each morning you photograph it, give it a colour score and count its brown spots.

materials.item: one yellow banana with no brown spots yet, and a second one if you want to compare it in a different place
a plate and a spot on a table out of direct sun
a notebook and pencil
a phone camera, if you have one

projects.safety: Eat the banana by day 5 or 6, or put it in the compost or wet-waste bin if it gets too soft.

schedule.what: Write the plan. Put the banana on a plate. Photograph it, score its colour and count its spots.
Same time, same place: photo, score, spot count.
Photo, score, spot count.
Photo, score, spot count.
Last look. Put the five records in a row. Draw a bar chart of the spots.

projects.record: A table with the day, the time, the colour score, the number of spots and a drawing or photo, every morning for five days.

flow.do: 1. Write the plan with your child: question, guess and why, what to look at, how often, how to record. 2. Put the banana on a plate on the table, out of direct sun. 3. First photo, colour score and spot count.
flow.say: Our question: how fast does a banana get brown spots? What's your guess? We'll look every morning at the same time. Count the spots, score the colour, take a photo.
flow.kid: Write your plan. Put the banana on the plate. Count its brown spots. Take a photo. Write the time.

ask.q: How often should we look at a banana, and why not every ten minutes?
good: Once a day, because bananas change slowly.
Every ten minutes we'd see nothing new.

flow.context: This is the first step of One Banana, Five Days. You write a plan and make the first record of a ripening banana.

flow.do: Each morning, at the same time, take a photo, score the colour and count the spots.
flow.say: Banana time. Same place, same time. How many spots today?
flow.kid: Count today's spots. Score the colour. Take a photo. Write it down.
flow.wait: Look again tomorrow morning, and every morning until day 5.
flow.parent: When the spots join together, counting gets hard. Then write 'too many to count' and give a colour score instead. That is a real problem scientists meet, and choosing a new way to record is good thinking.

flow.do: On day 5, put the five photos or drawings in a row. Draw a bar chart of the spot counts.
flow.say: Let's look at all five days. When did the spots grow fastest? What do you think would happen by day 8?
flow.kid: Put your five days in a row. Draw a bar for each day's spots. When did they grow fastest?

check.q: Sundari's banana had 0 spots on day 1, 2 on day 2, 6 on day 3 and 15 on day 4. What happened to the spots?
options: They grew by the same number each day
check.why: From day 1 to 2 the spots went up by 2, then by 4, then by 9. Each day more new spots appeared than the day before. One look on day 4 could never show that. Only a record of every day can.

setup.art: A yellow banana on a white plate on a table, with a notebook open beside it showing a table with Day, Time, Score and Spots.
setup.caption: 1. Plan it. Put the banana on a plate. First record.

setup.art: Five photos of the same banana in a row, from yellow to heavily spotted, labelled Day 1 to Day 5.
setup.caption: 2. Every morning, same time: photo, score and spots.

setup.art: A child's bar chart with five bars getting taller, labelled Day 1 to Day 5, Brown spots.
setup.caption: 3. On day 5, draw a bar chart and compare.

projects.title: A Tree From My Window: one month
projects.context: In this month-long project you choose a tree you can see from your window or balcony, and look at it once a week. You record its leaves, flowers, fruit and visitors.

materials.item: a tree you can see from home, or a potted plant if no tree is in view
a notebook for drawings
a phone camera, if you have one

projects.safety: Watch from inside the window or the balcony. If you go down to the tree, a grown-up comes too.

schedule.what: Choose the tree. Draw it. Write what you see: leaves, flowers, fruit, birds or insects.
Second look: draw and write the same things.
Third look.
Fourth look.
Last look. Compare the four weeks.

projects.record: Each week, the date, a drawing, and answers to the same four questions: new leaves? flowers? fruit? visitors?

flow.do: 1. Choose a tree you can see from home. 2. Decide the four questions you will answer each week. 3. Make the first drawing and record.
flow.say: This tree will be our study for a month. Every week we'll answer the same four questions. Same questions every time, so we can compare.
flow.kid: Pick your tree. Draw it. Answer four questions: new leaves? Flowers? Fruit? Visitors?
flow.parent: In Indian cities you may be watching a neem, gulmohar, mango, coconut or peepal. If no tree can be seen, use a potted plant. The SeasonWatch project, run by the Nature Conservation Foundation, collects exactly this kind of weekly tree record from children across India. You can send yours there too.
flow.context: This is the first step of A Tree From My Window. You choose a tree and make the first of four weekly records.

flow.do: Each week, answer the same four questions and make a drawing.
flow.say: Tree day. Same four questions. Anything new?
flow.kid: Look at your tree. Answer the four questions. Draw it.
flow.wait: Look again next week, for four weeks in all.

flow.do: After four weeks, compare all the records.
flow.say: What changed in a month? Did anything change that you never noticed on a single day?
flow.kid: Look at all four weeks. What changed?
flow.think: SeasonWatch has records from many years. What could many years show that one month cannot?

setup.art: A child at a flat window drawing a neem tree across the road in a notebook.
setup.caption: 1. Choose a tree you can see. Draw it.

setup.art: Four drawings of the same tree, labelled Week 1 to Week 4, with new leaves and a bird's nest appearing.
setup.caption: 2. Once a week, answer the same four questions.

challenges.title: Catch the Sunny Patch
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. Sunlight through a window makes a bright patch on the floor that moves slowly. You design a way to record its journey without sitting and watching all the time.
challenges.problem: On a sunny day, the bright patch from a window creeps across the floor. It moves too slowly to see. How can you record where it goes over two hours, while still doing other things?
constraints: You may not sit and watch the whole time.
Your record must show where the patch was and at what time.
Don't put tape where it may peel paint, and ask before marking the floor.
materials: paper, newspaper or old chart paper
a phone camera, if you have one
general: Lay a big sheet of paper or newspaper on the floor where the patch is, and trace its edge every 15 minutes, writing the time on each outline.
Put a small piece of tape at one corner of the patch every 15 minutes, with the time written on it.
Take a photo from the same spot every 15 minutes.
creative: Put a steel tumbler in the patch and draw the edge of its shadow every 15 minutes. The shadow moves as the patch does.
Set a phone to take a time-lapse video from a chair, and watch two hours in a few seconds.
Trace the patch in a different colour each time, so the outlines make a rainbow fan.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own way to record the sunny patch. Draw your plan, try it for two hours, and show your record. What does it show that one look could not?

flow.do: On a sunny morning, find a bright patch from a window on the floor. Watch it for one minute.
flow.say: Look at this sunny patch. Watch its edge for one minute. Does it move?
flow.kid: Find the sunny patch on the floor. Watch its edge for one minute. Does it move?
flow.context: This is the first step of Catch the Sunny Patch. You see the problem: the patch moves too slowly to see.

flow.do: Draw three ideas for recording the patch without watching all the time. Choose one.
flow.say: Engineers draw before they build. What are three ways to record where the patch goes, and when?
flow.kid: Draw three ideas. How can you record the patch without watching all the time? Pick one.

ask.q: How often will you mark the patch, and why that often?
good: Every 15 minutes, because it moves slowly.
Every 10 minutes, so I can see small steps.

flow.do: Carry out the plan for about two hours. Each mark takes about two minutes.
flow.say: Time to mark it. Write the time on the mark.
flow.kid: Mark the patch. Write the time. Go and play. Come back for the next mark.
flow.parent: The patch moves because the Earth turns, so the Sun's direction changes through the day. On a cloudy day, try another day. A window facing east is best in the morning, and one facing west in the afternoon.

flow.do: Read the usual and creative solutions together, then improve your own.
flow.say: Here are some usual ways and some creative ones. Could you make yours better?
flow.kid: Look at the usual ideas and some creative ones. Could you make yours better?
flow.think: Long ago, people used a stick's moving shadow to tell the time. How is that like your record?

setup.art: A bright patch of sunlight on a tiled floor below a window, with a child kneeling beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Find the sunny patch. Watch it for a minute.

setup.art: A sheet of newspaper on the floor with five pencil outlines of the patch in a fan, each labelled with a time.
setup.caption: 2. Mark its edge every 15 minutes, with the time.

challenges.title: The Plan Swap
challenges.context: This is a writing and testing challenge. You write a plan so clear that someone else can follow it without asking you anything, and get the same result.
challenges.problem: A scientist's plan must be so clear that another scientist, somewhere else, can repeat the test and check the result. Can you write an apple-slice plan that a grown-up can follow exactly, without asking you a single question?
constraints: Your plan must fit on one page.
The person following it may not ask you anything.
They must be able to say what to compare, what to keep the same, how often to look and how to record.
materials: a sheet of paper and a pencil
an apple, a lemon, water and a bowl, for the person who follows the plan
general: Give amounts and times: 'three slices, each as thick as a pencil', 'every 10 minutes for 60 minutes'.
Draw the results table for them.
creative: Add small pictures beside each step, like a recipe card.
Add a 'what to do if' line: what to do if the plain slice stays pale.
Ask two people to follow the same plan, and see if they get the same scores.
challenges.your_turn: Now write your own plan for a different slow change, like a banana ripening, and swap it with someone. Could they follow it without asking you anything?

flow.do: Your child writes a one-page plan for the brown apple watch, from memory and their own notes.
flow.say: Write a plan so clear that I could do the apple test without asking you anything. Every step, every amount, every time.
flow.kid: Write the apple plan for a grown-up. Every step. Every amount. Every time. They can't ask you anything!
flow.context: This is the first step of the Plan Swap. You write a plan for someone else to follow.

flow.do: The grown-up follows the plan exactly, doing only what is written. When something is missing, they stop and say what they don't know.
flow.say: I'll follow your plan exactly, word for word. If something is missing, I'll stop and tell you.
flow.kid: Watch the grown-up follow your plan. Where do they get stuck?
flow.parent: Be strict but kind. If the plan says 'cut slices' without saying how many, say 'How many?' and wait for your child to add it. The gaps are the lesson. You don't need to run the full hour: following the plan up to the first two looks is enough.

flow.do: Your child fixes the plan wherever the grown-up got stuck. Read the usual and creative ideas together.
flow.say: Where did I get stuck? Let's fix those parts. Here are some ideas other plan writers use.
flow.kid: Fix the parts where the grown-up got stuck. Look at the other ideas. Would they help?

check.q: Why do scientists want other people to be able to repeat their tests?
options: So they can copy the answer
So others can check whether the result really happens
check.why: If someone else follows the same plan and gets the same result, the result is much more trustworthy. If they get a different result, something needs checking. That is why scientists write their plans clearly in their reports.

setup.art: A child writing a numbered plan on a sheet of paper, with small pictures of an apple, a lemon and a clock.
setup.caption: 1. Write a plan so clear nobody needs to ask.

setup.art: A father reading the plan at the kitchen counter, holding a knife and an apple, looking puzzled at one line.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up follows it exactly. Where do they get stuck?
