quiz.p: Anjali, a girl in Class 3, wonders about her money plant. Which question can she find out by watching?
opts: Does the money plant grow a new leaf every week?
quiz.why: She can count the leaves every week and compare. The other two questions are real, but watching alone can't answer them.

quiz.p: Before cutting the apple, why do we write down our guess?
opts: So we can't change it after we see the result
quiz.why: Once you have seen the result, it is easy to think you knew it all along. A written guess keeps you honest, and a wrong guess is often the most interesting part.

quiz.p: In the apple test, why are all three slices cut from the same apple?
opts: So the only difference is plain, lemon or water
Because one apple is enough to eat
quiz.why: Different apples can brown at different speeds. Using one apple keeps that the same, so the only difference between the slices is the one you chose.

quiz.p: Vidya wants to know how fast her tomato plant grows. How often should she measure it?
quiz.why: A tomato plant grows a little each day, so measuring every few days shows clear steps. Every minute shows nothing new. Every five years misses the plant's whole life.

quiz.p: What should every line of a record have?
opts: The name of a famous scientist
quiz.why: Without the time, you can't say how long a change took or put the looks in order. Each line should also have what you saw, as a score, a drawing or a few words.

quiz.p: Kavya stared at her apple slice for a minute and saw nothing change. But her drawings every 10 minutes showed it going brown. What does this show?
opts: Some changes are too slow to see, but a record over time catches them
The apple only browns when nobody looks
quiz.why: In one minute the change is too small for the eye. Ten-minute steps are big enough to see when the drawings are side by side. The apple browns whether or not anyone is looking.

quiz.p: Farhan and his mother remember last week's apple test differently. How can they settle it?
opts: The one who is older is right
Look at the record they wrote during the test
Do whatever they both agree on
quiz.why: Memory can change without our noticing, for anyone of any age. The record made at the time doesn't change, so it settles the question.

quiz.p: Why does a cut apple turn brown?
opts: An enzyme from broken cells helps the apple's substances join with oxygen from the air
Light from the room paints it brown
quiz.why: Cutting breaks the cells, the enzyme and the colourless substances mix, and oxygen joins in to make brown substances. It happens in the dark too, and far too quickly for germs to be the cause.

quiz.p: Why does lemon juice keep an apple slice pale?
opts: It is sour, and the browning enzyme works slowly in sour juice
It is yellow, so it hides the brown
quiz.why: Lemon juice is acidic, and the enzyme works slowly in acid. Its vitamin C also undoes the first step of browning. It doesn't hide the colour or cool the slice.

quiz.p: A slice kept in the fridge browns more slowly than one on the table. Why?
opts: There is no air in a fridge
quiz.why: A fridge is full of air, and the apple browns in the dark too. The cold slows the enzyme down, so the browning is slower.

quiz.p: In 1572, what did Tycho Brahe find when he measured the new star night after night?
opts: It moved quickly across the sky
It never shifted against the stars near it
It was a cloud of smoke
quiz.why: A near thing seems to shift a little against far stars as the Earth turns. The new star never shifted, so it was far beyond the Moon.

quiz.p: What old idea did Tycho Brahe's new star show was wrong?
opts: That the sky beyond the Moon never changes
quiz.why: Many people in Europe followed Aristotle, who taught that the sky beyond the Moon was perfect and unchanging. A new star far beyond the Moon showed that the sky can change.

items.p: Meenakshi, a girl in Class 3 in Madurai, wonders about the ants in her kitchen. Which of her questions can she find out at home by watching or testing?
opts: Why are there ants in the world?
Do the ants reach a grain of sugar or a grain of rice first?
items.why: Meenakshi can put a grain of sugar and a grain of rice near the ant trail and watch which one the ants reach first. The other two questions are real and interesting, but one test at home can't answer them. A strong answer says what she would actually do.

items.p: Lakshmi says, 'If I stare at a cut apple slice for one minute, I will see it turn brown.' Is she right?
items.why: False. The slice is changing, but in one minute the change is too small for the eye to notice. Looking every 10 minutes and comparing the drawings shows it clearly.

items.p: Looking at something carefully, and using your other senses too, is called ____.
a: observing
observation
observe
items.why: To observe is to notice carefully with your eyes, ears, nose and hands. Each thing you notice is an observation.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: a guess with a reason, made before the test
what you write or draw at the time you look
the time between one look and the next
what you actually saw, counted or measured
only one thing is different, everything else is the same
items.why: These five words are the tools of finding out. A strong answer could also give an example from the apple test for each one.

items.p: Put the steps of the brown apple watch in order.
items: Cut three slices at the same time
Write your guess and your reason
Score and draw each slice every 10 minutes
Make the colour card and the table
Compare the drawings in a row
a: Make the colour card and the table
Write your guess and your reason
Cut three slices at the same time
Score and draw each slice every 10 minutes
Compare the drawings in a row
items.why: The plan and the guess come first, before anything is cut, so the guess can't be changed after seeing the result. Then the test, then the looks, then the comparing.

items.p: Sort these questions. Can you answer each with one look, or do you need a long watch over time?
items: What colour is a tomato's inside?
One look
Does our tulsi plant grow a new leaf each week?
Long watch
How many windows does our room have?
One look
Does the Moon change shape over a month?
Long watch
Is the steel tumbler shiny?
One look
How fast does a banana get brown spots?
Long watch
items.why: Anything about how something changes needs a long watch, with looks at set times. A question about how something is right now needs only one look.

items.p: Farhan wants to watch a banana ripen. How often should he look?
items.why: A banana changes over about a week. Looking once a day gives five or six looks, each showing a small, clear step. Every 10 minutes he would see nothing new for hours. Once a year he would miss it completely.

items.p: Kavya says she doesn't need to write anything down during the apple test, because she will remember it. Write two reasons why a scientist writes things down at the time.
items.a: Memory changes, and fills gaps with what we expect, so we can remember wrongly without knowing. A record made at the time stays the same, so we can compare looks, and other people can check what we saw.
items.why: A strong answer gives two different reasons: memory can be wrong, and a record can be checked and compared. A very strong answer gives an example, like the Spot the Change game.

items.p: Draw the three apple slices from the brown apple watch as they looked after one hour: plain, lemon and under water. Colour them and write each one's score.
items.a: The plain slice brown or light brown (score 2 or 3), the lemon slice still cream (score 0), and the water slice pale or a little yellow (score 0 or 1).
items.why: Results vary with the kind of apple. A strong drawing shows the plain slice browner than both others, and the lemon slice palest, and matches the child's own record.
items.art: Three empty slice outlines on a plate, labelled plain, lemon and water.

items.p: The plain apple slice browned faster than the slice under water. What did the air give the plain slice that the water slice mostly didn't get?
items.why: The browning needs oxygen from the air. Water keeps most of it away. Both slices were in the same light and warmth, so those can't explain the difference. Dust is too little to matter.

items.p: Arjun's apple slice has gone brown after an hour on the plate. It is safe to eat.
items.why: True. Browning is a change in the apple's own substances with oxygen. It is not rotting. Mould, slime or a bad smell would be signs of rotting.

items.p: Two sisters in Kochi are planning the apple test. They disagree about when to look.

views.says: Let's look only at the start and after one hour. That's enough to see which slice went brown.
Let's look every 10 minutes. Then we see when each slice started to change, and how fast.

items.ask: Which sister do you agree with? Give a reason. Then say one good thing about the other sister's plan.
items.a: A strong answer sees that Kavya's plan is quicker and does show which slice ended up browner. Meena's plan also shows when and how fast each slice changed, which two looks can't show.
items.why: Both plans answer a question, but not the same question. A strong answer says what each plan can and can't tell you, and chooses the one that fits the question asked.

items.p: Which of these is NOT part of a plan for the apple test?
items.why: How often, what stays the same and how to record are all parts of a good plan. The colour of your T-shirt makes no difference to the apple.

items.p: Divya wonders, 'Why does our dosa batter get bubbly?' Turn her wondering into a question she could find out by watching or testing.
items.a: For example: 'Does the batter rise more in a warm place or in the fridge overnight?' or 'How much higher is the batter after 4 hours, 8 hours and 12 hours?'
items.why: A strong question says what to look at or measure, and what to compare or how often to look.

items.p: The time you wait between one look and the next is called the ____.
a: interval
items.why: Choose the interval to match how fast the thing changes: short for an apple slice, a day for a banana.

items.p: Arjun cut his plain slice from a red apple and his lemon slice from a green apple. The lemon slice stayed paler. What is wrong with his test?
opts: Nothing, it is a fair test
Two things were different, so he can't tell if the lemon or the apple made the difference
He should have used more lemon
items.why: In a fair test only one thing differs. Arjun changed the apple and the lemon at once. Some kinds of apple brown more slowly than others, so the green apple alone might explain it. All slices should come from one apple.

items.p: Lakshmi did the apple test but looked only once, after five hours. All three slices were brown. She says, 'Lemon doesn't work.' What went wrong with her plan, and how should she fix it?
items.a: She looked too late, so she missed the time when the lemon slice was still pale and the others were brown. Lemon slows browning, but after many hours even a lemon slice may brown. She should look every 10 minutes for the first hour.
items.why: A strong answer sees that the interval and the length of the watch were wrong for the question, not the lemon. Slowing a change is not the same as stopping it.

items.p: Here is part of Revathi's apple record. Plain slice: 1 at 20 minutes, 2 at 30 minutes. Water slice: 0 at 20 minutes, 0 at 30 minutes. Which slice changed between 20 and 30 minutes?
items.why: The plain slice went from score 1 to score 2. The water slice stayed at 0. Reading a record line by line shows exactly when each change happened.

items.p: Lemon juice keeps an apple slice pale only because it covers the slice and keeps the air out.
items.why: False. A slice wet with plain water still browns in the air. Lemon works mainly because it is sour, or acidic, and the browning enzyme works slowly in acid. Its vitamin C also undoes the first step of the browning.

items.p: The gas from the air that helps a cut apple turn brown is called ____.
a: oxygen
items.why: Oxygen joins with the apple's colourless substances, helped by the enzyme, to make the brown ones.

items.p: Kavya tests whether a slice browns more slowly in the fridge. Sort these into what she changes and what she keeps the same.
items: where the slice is: fridge or table
Changes
which apple the slices come from
Keeps the same
how thick the slices are
Keeps the same
when the slices are cut
Keeps the same
the colour card she uses
Keeps the same
how often she looks
Keeps the same
items.why: Only one thing changes: fridge or table. Everything else stays the same, so any difference must come from the cold.

items.p: Remember Farzana in the story, who checked the crack in the wall. Put her plan in order.
items: Check every Sunday and after heavy rain
Draw pencil lines past both ends and write the date
Ask exactly what the question is: longer, wider or both?
Compare six weeks of records
Glue a paper strip across the widest part
a: Ask exactly what the question is: longer, wider or both?
Draw pencil lines past both ends and write the date
Glue a paper strip across the widest part
Check every Sunday and after heavy rain
Compare six weeks of records
items.why: A clear question comes first, because it decides what to mark. Then the marks, then regular looks, then comparing the record.

items.p: Two friends in Mysuru are keeping records of a banana ripening. They argue about the best record.

views.says: A drawing is best. When you draw, you have to look closely, so you notice more.
A photo is best. It shows exactly what was there, and you can't get it wrong.

items.ask: Which friend do you agree with? Give a reason. Then answer back from the other side.
items.a: A strong answer sees that a photo is exact and quick but can miss what you didn't notice, while a drawing makes you look closely but can be inaccurate. Many scientists use both.
items.why: There is no single right answer. Each kind of record is good at something different. A strong answer uses an example from the child's own records.

items.p: Draw a plan card for the banana diary. Show your question, how often you will look, what you will count, and how you will record it.
items.a: A card with a question (for example 'How fast does the banana get brown spots?'), 'every morning at 8', 'count spots and score the colour', and a small table or photo plan.
items.why: A strong plan card says what, how often, how long and how to record, so someone else could follow it.
items.art: A blank card with four empty boxes labelled Question, How often, What I count, How I record.

items.p: Why should you look at the apple slices in the same light every time?
opts: So a change in the light doesn't look like a change in the apple
Because apples only brown in lamplight
items.why: Window light changes through the day. A slice can look darker in dim light even if it hasn't changed. Keeping the light the same is part of keeping the test fair.

items.p: The slice under water browned more slowly than the plain slice. Explain why, using the word oxygen.
items.a: The browning needs oxygen from the air. Water keeps most of the air away from the slice, so less oxygen reaches it, and it browns more slowly.
items.why: A strong answer links the slow browning to less oxygen, not to the water itself doing something to the apple.

items.p: Match each slow change to a good interval between looks.
items.why: Each interval gives several looks during the change, each showing a small step. Faster changes need shorter intervals.

items.p: Label this record page: the time, the colour score, the drawing, and the notes.
items.a: The time is in the first column, the colour score in the second, a small drawing of the slice in the third, and a few words about what was noticed in the last.
items.why: Every look in a good record has a time, a measurement or score, a picture and notes, so it can be compared with the other looks.
items.art: A notebook page with a four-column table and blank labels pointing to each column.

items.p: Three of these turn brown for the same reason as a cut apple. Which is the odd one out?
items.why: Cut potato, brinjal and banana all brown because broken cells let an enzyme and oxygen work. Toast browns because of heat, which is a different change.

items.p: You hold a pencil at arm's length and swap eyes. The pencil seems to jump, but a far building does not. What does this show?
opts: Near things seem to shift when you look from a different place, far things don't
items.why: Your two eyes look from slightly different places. Something near seems to jump against the far background. Something very far does not. Tycho used this idea to show the new star was far beyond the Moon.

items.p: Ruksana wonders, 'Does a banana ripen faster inside a closed paper bag?' Write a full plan for her: the question, a guess and why, what to compare, what to keep the same, how often to look and how to record it.
items.a: For example: two bananas from the same bunch, equally yellow. One in a closed paper bag, one beside it on the plate. Same room, same table. Look every morning at 8 for five days. Count the spots and take a photo of each, taking the bagged one out only for a moment.
items.why: A strong plan has every part: a clear question, a guess with a reason, two things compared, a list of what stays the same, an interval matched to a banana, and a way to record.

items.p: In 1572, a new star appeared in the sky. Two people disagree about what it is.

views.says: The sky beyond the Moon never changes. So this new light must be in the air, nearer than the Moon.
I measured it night after night. It never shifts against the other stars, as a near thing would. So it is far beyond the Moon.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with? Use the idea of near things seeming to shift. Then answer back as the other person would have done.
items.a: A strong answer sides with Tycho because of his measurements, but can also argue that the follower of Aristotle trusted a teaching that had seemed to work for a very long time, and might have doubted Tycho's instrument.
items.why: Tycho had evidence from a planned test. The other view rested on an old teaching. A strong answer explains why measurements can overturn a famous idea, and is fair to the other side.

items.p: In Farhan's apple test, he cut the plain slice first, and the lemon slice 20 minutes later. After one hour, the plain slice was browner. What is the problem?
opts: The plain slice had 20 minutes more time to brown
items.why: The plain slice had 60 minutes in the air and the lemon slice only 40. So the time, not just the lemon, could explain the difference. All slices must start at the same time.

items.p: In the story, Farzana checked the crack for six weeks, and it never changed. Her brother said the test was a waste of time. Was it? Explain.
items.a: It was not a waste. 'No change' is a real answer. It showed Abba's memory was wrong, so the family did not need to worry, and the marks will show at once if the crack ever starts to grow.
items.why: A strong answer sees that finding no change is a result, and that it settled an argument that memory could not settle.

items.p: Divya looks at her apple slices only at 0, 30 and 60 minutes. What might she miss?
opts: When each slice started to brown, and how fast it changed in between
items.why: With three looks she can still see which slice was browner at the end. But if the plain slice browned between 0 and 30 minutes, she can't tell whether it took 10 minutes or 25. More looks show the change in smaller steps.

items.p: If two people remember the same thing differently, one of them must be lying.
items.why: False. Honest people often remember the same thing differently, because memory fills gaps without our noticing. That is why a record made at the time is so useful.

items.p: Draw what you think two apple slices would look like after one hour: one kept in the fridge and one left on the table. Label each one and give it a colour score.
items.a: The table slice browner (score 2 or 3) and the fridge slice paler (score 0 or 1).
items.why: Cold slows the enzyme, so the fridge slice browns more slowly. A strong drawing labels both and gives scores that match this.
items.art: Two empty slice outlines, one inside a drawn fridge shelf and one on a drawn table.

items.p: A star that explodes, and shines very brightly for a while before fading, is called a ____.
a: supernova
items.why: The new star Tycho Brahe watched in 1572 was a supernova. Telescopes today can still see the cloud of gas it left.

items.p: After the apple test, people said these things. Sort them: is each one evidence from the test, or not?
items: 'My drawing at 30 minutes shows the plain slice at score 2.'
Evidence
'I'm sure it was darker than that.'
Not evidence
'The photo at 60 minutes shows the lemon slice still cream.'
Evidence
'I hoped the water slice would win.'
Not evidence
'My table says the water slice reached 1 at 40 minutes.'
Evidence
'Everyone knows apples go brown.'
Not evidence
items.why: Evidence is what was recorded at the time: drawings, photos and table entries. Feelings, hopes and what 'everyone knows' are not evidence from this test.

items.p: When you bite an apple and leave it, the brown appears first around the tooth marks. Why there?
opts: That is where the cells were broken open
items.why: The browning starts where cells are broken, because that is where the enzyme and the colourless substances mix and meet oxygen. A whole, unbroken apple stays cream inside.

items.p: Your steel tumbler looks exactly the same as it did last year. Is it changing at all? Give your reasons.
items.a: It may be changing very slowly: getting tiny scratches, wearing thin where it is scrubbed, or getting a dent. One look can't show it, but photos over many years might.
items.why: A strong answer uses the idea from the apple test: a change can be real and still too slow to see, and a record over time can show it.

items.p: Put Tycho Brahe's test of the new star in order.
items: He concluded it was far beyond the Moon
He saw a bright new star in Cassiopeia
He measured its position against nearby stars, night after night
He asked: is it nearer or further than the Moon?
He found it never shifted
a: He saw a bright new star in Cassiopeia
He asked: is it nearer or further than the Moon?
He measured its position against nearby stars, night after night
He found it never shifted
He concluded it was far beyond the Moon
items.why: Noticing comes first, then a clear question, then a planned measurement repeated over time, then the result, then what it means.

items.p: Why did Tycho measure the new star on many nights, instead of just once?
opts: A single measurement could be a mistake, and many matching ones are much stronger evidence
The star was only visible every other night
items.why: One measurement could be thrown off by a shaky hand or a cloud. Many measurements that agree are strong evidence. He also wanted to see whether the star changed over time, and it slowly faded.

items.p: Which of these is NOT a record?
opts: A photo taken at each look
A tally sheet filled in at the window
A table written during the test
What you remember about it next week
items.why: A record is made at the time and does not change afterwards. A memory recalled next week can change without you knowing.

items.p: A slice of apple under an upside-down steel bowl gets no air, so it stays pale.
items.why: False. The air trapped under the bowl still has plenty of oxygen. The slice usually browns almost as fast as one in the open. Under water, much less oxygen reaches the slice.

applications: Weather scientists record rainfall and temperature every day, and long records show how the climate is changing.
Doctors chart a patient's temperature every few hours to see whether a fever is going up or down.
Engineers mark cracks in bridges and buildings and check them for months to see whether they are growing.
Farmers note when crops flower and when pests appear, so they can plan the next season.
Astronomers photograph the same patch of sky night after night to find new stars, comets and asteroids.
Cooks keep cut potato and brinjal in water, and put lemon on cut fruit, to slow browning.
Teachers and parents mark a child's height on a wall chart each year.
Wildlife scientists count birds at the same place every year to see whether their numbers are rising or falling.
Food scientists test new ways to keep cut fruit fresh, using the same kind of plan as the apple test.

open_questions.q: Exactly what jobs does the browning enzyme do inside a healthy apple tree?
open_questions.why_open: Many scientists think it helps defend damaged fruit and leaves against insects and germs. But the enzyme is also found in healthy parts of the plant. Its other jobs there are still being studied.

open_questions.q: Why does memory change over time, and can we stop it?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know memories are rebuilt each time we recall them, and can pick up new details. How this happens in the brain is still being worked out.

open_questions.q: Which stars in our part of the galaxy will explode next, and when?
open_questions.why_open: Astronomers know some stars that will one day become supernovas, like the red giant Betelgeuse. But they can't yet say whether that will be in a hundred years or a hundred thousand.

open_questions.q: How many slow changes around us has nobody ever recorded?
open_questions.why_open: Many slow changes in soil, rocks, trees and animals have only been watched for a few years, or not at all. Long records, kept for decades, are rare and precious.

open_questions.q: How small a change can the human eye notice?
open_questions.why_open: It depends on the light, the colour and the person. Scientists have measured it in labs, but in everyday life it varies a lot, which is one more reason to use records.

maths.problem: In the brown apple watch, Revathi looks at her slices at 0 minutes, then every 10 minutes until 60 minutes. How many looks is that?
maths.explain: She looks at 0, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 and 60 minutes. That is 7 looks. Counting in tens from 10 to 60 gives 6, and the first look at 0 makes 7. It is easy to forget the start.
maths.context: This is about the brown apple watch, where you score apple slices every 10 minutes for an hour.
maths.why_maths: Counting the looks before you start tells you how many rows your table needs, so you don't run out of space.

maths.problem: Divya cut her apple at 4:15 in the afternoon. Her plain slice reached score 2 at 4:45. How long did it take?
maths.explain: From 4:15 to 4:45, the minute hand moves from 15 to 45. 45 minus 15 is 30. So it took 30 minutes.
maths.context: This is about the brown apple watch, where you write the time at every look.
maths.why_maths: A record shows how fast a change happens only if you can work out the time between two looks.

maths.problem: Tycho Brahe saw the new star in November 1572. It faded from sight in March 1574. About how many months could it be seen?
maths.explain: From November 1572 to November 1573 is 12 months. From November 1573 to March 1574 is 4 more months: December, January, February and March. 12 and 4 make 16.
maths.context: This is about Tycho Brahe, who watched a new star in the sky for as long as it could be seen.
maths.why_maths: Counting months on a calendar turns 'a long time' into an exact number, so we can compare it with other stars.

maths.problem: Sundari counted the brown spots on her banana each morning: 0, 2, 6, 15. How many new spots appeared each day? Do you think day 5 will have more or fewer than 25 spots?
maths.answer: 2, then 4, then 9 new spots. Day 5 will probably have more than 25.
maths.explain: From 0 to 2 is 2 new spots. From 2 to 6 is 4 new. From 6 to 15 is 9 new. The number of new spots grows each day, so on day 5 probably more than 9 new spots appear. 15 and 10 is 25, so day 5 probably has more than 25. The spots may soon join up and be too many to count.
maths.context: This is about One Banana, Five Days, where you count a banana's brown spots every morning.

chart.title: Brown spots on Sundari's banana (made-up example)

maths.why_maths: Finding how much the count grows each day shows whether the change is speeding up, and lets you predict what comes next.

maths.problem: In the Window Watch, Kavya counted crows for one minute at three times: 6 crows at 7 in the morning, 1 at 1 in the afternoon, 4 at 5 in the evening. How many more crows came at 7 than at 1? Can she say crows always come less at 1 o'clock?
maths.answer: 5 more crows. She can't say 'always' from one day.
maths.explain: 6 minus 1 is 5. But one day can be a fluke: maybe a loud lorry passed at 1 o'clock. To be sure of a pattern, she needs to count at the same times on many days.
maths.context: This is about the Window Watch, where you tally what you see from one window for one minute every two hours.
maths.why_maths: Subtracting shows how big the difference is, and asking whether one day is enough shows what the numbers can and can't tell us.

maths.problem: Arjun wants to check his banana every 10 minutes for one whole day of 12 hours. There are 6 lots of 10 minutes in an hour. How many looks would that be? Is it a good plan?
maths.answer: 72 looks. It is not a good plan for a banana.
maths.explain: 6 looks an hour for 12 hours is 6 times 12, which is 72. A banana changes so slowly that almost every look would show nothing new. One look a day is enough.
maths.context: This is about choosing how often to look, which is called the interval.
maths.why_maths: Working out the number of looks before you start shows whether a plan is sensible or far too much work.

roots.context: We have planned a test and watched apple slices turn brown over an hour, and heard how Tycho Brahe watched a new star. Now we ask what slow changes tell us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: Each time you glanced at the plain apple slice, it looked the same as a moment before. Yet your drawings from every ten minutes showed it turning brown. A change can be too slow for the eye, and still be real. So many things that look still are changing, only too slowly to see.
deep_truth.habit: We sort the world into things that change and things that stay still. But 'still' often only means 'changing more slowly than we look'. A record kept over time shows the change our eyes miss.
deep_truth.evidence: In one minute of staring, nobody saw the plain slice change. Laid side by side, the drawings made every ten minutes went from cream to brown. Tycho's nightly measurements showed the 'unchanging' sky changing too.

three.who_am_i: You are changing right now. Your hair grows about a centimetre a month, too slowly to see. Only a mark on the door frame shows how much you have grown.
three.what_is_life: Every living being is always changing: growing, healing, ripening and ageing, mostly too slowly for one look.
three.what_is_this_world: Even stars change. Tycho Brahe watched a new star blaze up and fade away over about a year and a half.

roots.thread: Your apple slice was one thing, yet your drawings show it as many: cream, yellow, light brown, brown. Each drawing is the same slice at a different moment. Laid in a row, they show one change unfolding. The world is like that. One world shows itself as countless moments, and a record lets us see how they belong together.

teachings.teaching: You cannot step into the same river twice.
teachings.link: A river looks the same from day to day, but the water in it is always new. The apple slice looked the same from minute to minute, but it was always changing.

teachings.teaching: All made things are impermanent. When one sees this with wisdom, one turns away from suffering.
teachings.link: The Buddha taught that nothing made stays the same. The apple, the banana and the new star of 1572 all show it, each at its own speed.

teachings.teaching: Whatever is said, by whoever says it, wisdom is to find the truth in it.
teachings.link: Aristotle was famous, but Tycho checked the sky for himself. In the apple test, your own record, not anyone's say-so, tells you what happened.

science.text: Many changes are too slow for our eyes. Time-lapse photos and long records let scientists see them.
Stars are born, change and die over millions or billions of years. A supernova is the sudden end of some stars.

other_view.view: Parmenides argued the opposite of Heraclitus. He said that what truly is cannot change, and that change is something our senses only seem to show us.

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if at home today, with the materials listed. Changes made: apple slices float, so the slice under water is held down by a small plate or katori, or its top browns in the air. Some apple kinds brown slowly, so the step says to wait longer or use a raw potato slice, which browns faster. Window light changes over an hour, so the looks use a lamp or the same spot each time. The fridge slice is taken out only for the few seconds of scoring. The banana diary says what to do when the spots join up and can't be counted. The sunny patch challenge needs a sunny day and names which window works best. The tree project gives a potted plant as the alternative when no tree is in view. Both games work for one child with a parent. The spine fits about 90 minutes over two sessions, with the hour of the apple test used for reading the explanation and Tycho Brahe cards between looks.

how_we_found_out.story: For about two thousand years, many people in Europe followed the Greek thinker Aristotle. He taught that the sky beyond the Moon is perfect and never changes. So any new light in the sky had to be something in the air, nearer than the Moon. In November 1572, a bright new star appeared in the group of stars called Cassiopeia. A young Danish astronomer, Tycho Brahe, saw it on 11 November. He made a plan to find out how far away it was. Something near, like the Moon, seems to shift a little against the far stars as the Earth turns through the night. Night after night, Tycho measured the new star's position against its neighbours, with a large instrument he had built. It never shifted. So it was far beyond the Moon, out among the stars. He kept watching as it faded over about sixteen months. In 1573 he published a small book, On the New Star. The sky could change after all. Today we know he had seen a supernova, an exploding star.
how_we_found_out.who: Tycho Brahe, a Danish astronomer, testing the old idea of Aristotle, a Greek thinker
how_we_found_out.when: November 1572 (the new star appears) to early 1574 (it fades from sight), and 1573 (Tycho's book De nova stella, On the New Star)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: People believed the sky beyond the Moon was perfect and could never change, so a new light had to be in the air, nearer than the Moon. Tycho's measurements showed the new star did not shift like a near thing, so it was far away among the stars.
